newsitem.title: USA: NY physical coffee - spot supply woes resurface.
newsitem.headline: NY physical coffee - spot supply woes resurface.

text.p: A sharp decline in U.S. coffee inventories revived concerns over the scarcity of nearby supplies and held New York spot differentials firm this week, traders said.

Stocks of exchange-deliverable coffee fell by 10,000 bags for the week ended September 27, to 31,669 bags, their lowest level in more than a decade, the Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange reported early this week.
"The CSCE stock data reinforces nearby supply concerns," one trader said. "Premiums for nearby coffee are holding up."
Following the stock decline, nearby December's premium to the outer contracts widened this week to more than 6.00 cents.
The sharp downturn in stocks comes just as roasters move into their heaviest processing period in October and November.
"We are getting cooler weather, which exacerbates the situation," a trader said.
But roaster buying remained somewhat tentative, with end-users reluctant to pay a premium for nearby shipments, counting on the ongoing Latin American harvest to replenish stockpiles.

"Dealers are selling forward for traditional prices and roasters are saying, why should I buy spots?" one trader said. "There a willingness by roasters to pay a premium for spot coffee only if there is a need."

Colombian MAMs for spot delivery were still relatively pricey at about 20 cents over December futures, little changed from a week ago. MAMs for forward delivery were also steady, ranging from 12 to 15 cents over for December-June delivery.
Elsewhere, hard-to-find spot Mexican beans fetched six cents over "C", up sharply from recent weeks. A small parcel of spot Honduran beans was offered at four cents over "C".
CSCE December coffee rose 2.35 cents a lb Friday, to settle at 109.80. March ended 1.85 higher, at 104.15.
